"Instead of disposing of garden prunings from your winter maintenance by burning or shredding them, consider transforming them into a dead hedge. This practical and eco-friendly solution serves multiple purposes: it functions as an effective windbreak, provides a safe haven for wildlife, and can even be used to create natural divisions within your garden space. To construct one, simply drive stakes or old fence posts into the ground in two parallel rows, spaced about 50 centimeters apart. Then, weave the pruned material between the posts, starting with the larger branches at the base. As you continue adding layers, the structure will gradually settle and become more compact over time.

Feeling disappointed with your Christmas gifts? Lift your spirits by pre-ordering *The Book of Seeds* (Ivy Press, £30), authored by Paul Smith, the former director of Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank. Set for release in February, this visually stunning book offers an in-depth look at 600 of the world’s most unusual and captivating seed species. Among its highlights are seeds with striking features, such as one with hair reminiscent of Donald Trump and another from an orchid so tiny it’s barely visible to the naked eye.

For those seeking winter beauty in their gardens, winter-flowering clematis is a remarkable choice. If planted in a sunny, sheltered location, these plants will reward you with vibrant blooms from December through February. Some standout varieties include *Clematis cirrhosa ‘Advent Bells’* (growing up to 3 meters tall and 1.5 meters wide) and *C. cirrhosa var. balearica* (reaching 2.5 meters by 1.5 meters), both of which produce creamy, fragrant flowers adorned with maroon speckles. Meanwhile, *C. cirrhosa ‘Jingle Bells’* offers pure white blossoms and can grow as large as 5 meters tall and 2 meters wide, making it an eye-catching addition to any garden."
